title: Civil Rights Division Hollowed Out: 368 Attorneys Quit as DOJ Targets Reverse Discrimination
synopsis: By July 2025, 368 employees had departed the DOJ Civil Rights Division since Trump's inauguration — an unprecedented exodus representing hundreds of thousands of years of combined experience, according to a congressional memo from Senator Peter Welch. Under Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, the division redirected its mission to investigating alleged reverse discrimination against white Americans, filing a lawsuit against Minnesota's affirmative action hiring policies. In June 2026, the DOJ's Office of Legal Counsel issued an opinion declaring disparate impact liability — the legal framework used to challenge policies that disproportionately harm minorities — unconstitutional, effectively immunizing policies with racially discriminatory effects. The EEOC dismissed multiple transgender discrimination cases, reversed protections for transgender workers, and its chair Andrea Lucas appealed directly to white men to file discrimination charges.

title: Pentagon Schools Quarantine Books on Race and Gender; DOE Drops Book-Ban Complaints
synopsis: On January 24, 2025, Trump's Education Department dismissed 11 complaints and six allegations related to school book bans filed during the Biden administration, calling them Biden's book ban hoax and eliminating its book ban coordinator position. PEN America had documented over 10,000 book bans in the 2023-2024 school year, nearly triple the prior year. Simultaneously, Pentagon schools serving 67,000 military children worldwide suspended all library access in February 2025 for a compliance review, quarantining books on gender, race, and LGBTQ themes — including To Kill a Mockingbird, Fahrenheit 451, and The Kite Runner. The ACLU sued on behalf of children on military bases in April 2025. On October 21, 2025, U.S. District Judge Patricia Tolliver Giles ruled the removals reflected improper partisan motivation and ordered the books immediately restored.

title: One Big Beautiful Bill Strips Healthcare From 10 Million, Bans Planned Parenthood from Medicaid
synopsis: On July 4, 2025, Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (P.L. 119-21), which the Congressional Budget Office projected would cut over $990 billion from Medicaid and CHIP over a decade and leave 10 million more Americans uninsured by 2034. The law imposed Medicaid work requirements that threatened to eliminate coverage for 2.1 million women of reproductive age, and barred refugees and asylum seekers from Medicaid eligibility. Section 71113 prohibited Planned Parenthood — which serves over one million Medicaid patients — from receiving federal Medicaid payments for one year, prompting Planned Parenthood to announce the closure of at least 32 clinics across 11 states. The administration also withheld Title X family planning funds from 12 grantees affecting close to 300 clinics starting April 1, 2025. The Senate passed the bill 51-50 with Vice President JD Vance casting the tiebreaking vote.

title: Alien Enemies Act Mass Disappearances: Men Loaded on Planes With 24 Hours Notice and No Lawyer
synopsis: Beginning March 14-15, 2025, the Trump administration invoked the 1798 Alien Enemies Act via Proclamation 10903 to summarily remove Venezuelan nationals alleged to be Tren de Aragua members — bypassing all standard immigration court procedures. The government loaded detainees onto planes while a federal court hearing was underway, with one detainee described as having been on a plane for about forty minutes before being retrieved after a court order. In J.G.G. v. Trump, the Supreme Court confirmed 9-0 that AEA detainees are entitled to due process notice within a reasonable time. On May 16, 2025, in A.A.R.P. v. Trump, a 7-2 Supreme Court ruling found that providing only 24 hours notice devoid of information about how to exercise due process rights surely does not pass muster. One deportee had no gang affiliation — he told the court his tattoos came from a Google image search because he thought it looked cool.

title: Medicaid Cuts Target Disabled Americans: $900B Slashed, States Begin Re-Institutionalizing
synopsis: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act signed July 4, 2025 cut a projected $900 billion-plus from Medicaid over a decade, and the June 2026 DOJ Olmstead opinion signaled the end of federal enforcement of community integration for people with disabilities. Iowa and other states began quietly reducing home health aide coverage and in-home support services that allow disabled people to avoid institutionalization. The Trump administration moved oversight of special education from the Department of Education to the Department of Health and Human Services under RFK Jr., whose public statements dismissing the severity of conditions like autism drew sharp rebukes from disability advocates. New Medicaid work requirements taking effect January 1, 2027 are expected to strip coverage from people with disabilities who cannot navigate complex exemption bureaucracies. Sen. Tammy Duckworth called the combination of cuts and DOJ opinion an attack on one of the most basic civil rights of Americans with disabilities.

title: ANWR Opened for Drilling on Inauguration Day
synopsis: On January 20, 2025, Trump signed Executive Order 14153, Unleashing Alaska's Extraordinary Resource Potential, immediately reversing Biden's halt on oil and gas drilling in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's Coastal Plain. The order reinstated the 2020 leasing program, directed the Interior Department to rescind lease cancellations and issue new permits, and denied a pending Indigenous sacred site designation in the Coastal Plain. The area, covering roughly 1.5 million acres, is sacred to the Gwich'in people who call it the Sacred Place Where Life Begins. Environmental groups warned the move would devastate calving grounds of the Porcupine caribou herd and accelerate Arctic warming.

title: EPA Slashes 23% of Workforce, Shuts Down Science Office
synopsis: On July 18, 2025, the EPA announced it was cutting at least 3,700 employees — 23% of its 16,155-person workforce — and permanently closing its Office of Research and Development, which employed roughly 1,500 scientists. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin framed the $748.8 million in projected savings as organizational improvements, but critics noted the agency's enforcement, Superfund, and water offices were all targeted. Earlier, in February 2025, the agency had placed 168 environmental justice staff on administrative leave. The restructuring effectively returned EPA staffing to 1980s Reagan-era levels, gutting the scientific independence underpinning pollution regulation.

title: Bears Ears and Grand Staircase Shrunk 90% to Open Mining
synopsis: On July 13, 2026, Trump signed proclamations reducing Bears Ears National Monument by 91% — from 1.36 million acres to 121,096 acres — and Grand Staircase-Escalante by roughly 90%, leaving just 182,000 of its original 1.87 million acres protected. The cuts, even deeper than Trump's 2017 reductions which Biden had restored, opened nearly 3 million acres to uranium mining, coal extraction, and oil drilling. Utah Mining Association president Brian Somers confirmed the Bear Ears region sits in Utah's uranium belt and Grand Staircase contains our largest coal reserves. Five tribes challenged the move, and legal groups argued the Antiquities Act is a one-way statute that prohibits presidential reduction of monuments.

title: Clean Water Act Gutted: Millions of Wetland Acres Stripped of Protection
synopsis: On November 17, 2025, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced a proposed rule dramatically narrowing the definition of Waters of the United States (WOTUS) under the Clean Water Act, removing federal protections from vast swaths of wetlands and seasonal waterways. The rule implemented the Supreme Court's 2023 Sackett v. EPA decision in the most expansive way possible, excluding intermittent streams, isolated wetlands, and groundwater from federal jurisdiction. Zeldin accused prior Democratic administrations of having weaponized water definitions against farmers and developers. Environmental groups warned the rollback would leave hundreds of millions of acres of wetlands — critical for flood control, clean water filtration, and wildlife — vulnerable to pollution and destruction.

title: Federal Climate Science Purged: National Climate Assessments Taken Offline
synopsis: In June and July 2025, the Trump administration systematically erased decades of federally mandated climate science. NOAA shut down climate.gov on June 24, 2025, pursuant to Trump's May 23 executive order Restoring Gold Standard Science. The U.S. Global Change Research Program website — hosting all five National Climate Assessments — went dark on July 1, 2025. NASA initially promised to host the reports but reversed course on July 14, stating it had no legal obligation to do so. All 400 experts working on the congressionally mandated Sixth National Climate Assessment had been dismissed in April 2025, along with $4 million in Princeton ocean modeling funding. Former NOAA scientist Haley Crim wrote: Federal climate science is being systematically erased.

title: Methane Fee Killed, Industry Given 18-Month Pollution Pass
synopsis: On March 14, 2025, Trump signed Public Law 119-2 revoking the EPA's methane waste emissions charge rule under the Congressional Review Act, eliminating a fee of $900-$1,500 per ton on excess methane releases from oil and gas operations. Congress passed the repeal along party lines on February 26-27, 2025. Then on July 31, 2025, EPA issued an interim final rule bypassing public comment to extend methane compliance deadlines by 18 months, which the agency's own fact sheet acknowledged would result in 3.8 million additional tons of methane emissions between 2028 and 2038 — equivalent to the emissions from 25 million gasoline-powered vehicles driven for a year — plus 960,000 tons of volatile organic compounds and 36,000 tons of toxic air pollutants.

title: Superfund Budget Slashed 47%, Toxic Site Cleanups Halted
synopsis: Trump's FY2026 budget request, released May 2, 2025, proposed cutting the EPA's Hazardous Substance Superfund account by $254.9 million — a 47.4% reduction from the FY2025 enacted level of $537.7 million. The Superfund Remedial program, historically the largest component, was zeroed out from discretionary appropriations entirely, with the administration betting that Superfund tax receipts — which had already fallen 26% short of projections — would cover cleanups at the National Priorities List's most toxic sites. State and Tribal Assistance Grants were cut by $3.6 billion, an 83% reduction. The overall EPA budget request of $4.2 billion represented a 54.5% cut from FY2025 enacted levels.

title: Wildfire Season Sabotaged: Forest Service Loses 5,000 Staff
synopsis: As the U.S. entered an above-normal fire year in 2025, the Trump administration's workforce cuts and funding freezes crippled federal wildfire response. Approximately 5,000 Forest Service employees — about 15% of the agency — departed in the first five months of the administration, leaving fire crews to fill support roles instead of fighting fires. Trump froze billions in congressionally appropriated wildfire mitigation funding tied to the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law and Inflation Reduction Act, halting over 30 active fuel-reduction contracts held by groups like Oregon's Lomakatsi Restoration Project. A February 14, 2025 ProPublica investigation found seasonal hiring frozen, training programs canceled, and prescribed burn crews turned back mid-mission. Firefighter captain Ben McLane described a massive sledgehammer hitting the force during prime training season.

title: EPA Proposes Repealing All Greenhouse Gas Rules for Power Plants, Weakening Mercury Limits
synopsis: On June 11, 2025, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced proposals to repeal all greenhouse gas emissions standards for fossil fuel-fired power plants under Section 111 of the Clean Air Act and to weaken the 2024 Mercury and Air Toxics Standards that had been driving coal plant retirements. Zeldin called climate change action a cult and said the rollback would save the power sector $19 billion over two decades. The proposal included a novel legal argument that EPA must first determine whether power plant greenhouse gas emissions contribute significantly to dangerous air pollution before regulating — effectively pre-determining that they do not. Environmental groups warned the rules would expose millions to mercury, arsenic, and lead while accelerating planetary warming.

title: National Petroleum Reserve Alaska Opened: 82% of 23 Million Acres Unlocked
synopsis: On November 13, 2025, the Trump administration finalized a rollback of Biden-era limits on oil and gas drilling in the National Petroleum Reserve in Alaska, the largest tract of undisturbed public land in the United States. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum rescinded a 2024 rule that had prohibited leasing on 10.6 million acres and restricted development on 2 million more, reopening 82% of the 23-million-acre reserve. The Bureau of Land Management immediately initiated a lease sale process for winter 2025 — the first since 2019 — mandated under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act signed July 4, 2025, which requires at least five lease sales by 2035 with each offering a minimum of 4 million acres. The reserve provides critical habitat for migratory birds, polar bears, and subsistence hunting communities.

title: FEMA Dismantled, Billion-Dollar Disaster Resilience Program Cancelled
synopsis: On April 3, 2025, an internal FEMA memo revealed the Trump administration's plan to cancel the Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities (BRIC) program — the federal government's largest-ever climate adaptation initiative — clawing back over $750 million in congressionally appropriated grants. Twenty states sued FEMA, arguing the cancellation violated federal law. On June 11, 2025, Trump announced plans to phase out FEMA entirely, saying We want to wean off of FEMA. FEMA staffing fell 9.5% between January and June 2025. The administration denied at least 12 state disaster aid requests along largely partisan lines, including California wildfire recovery funds, while approving aid for Republican-governed states.

title: Offshore Drilling Proposed Off California and Florida for First Time in Decades
synopsis: On November 20, 2025, the Interior Department unveiled an expansive 11th National Outer Continental Shelf Oil and Gas Leasing Program for 2026-2031, proposing up to 34 lease sales across 21 of 27 OCS planning areas covering approximately 1.27 billion acres. Critically, it included six lease sales off the California coast — where no federal leasing had occurred since 1984 — and new areas in the Gulf of America, Arctic, and Florida's Gulf coast. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said the plan replaced the smallest offshore leasing plan ever published. The proposal drew bipartisan opposition from coastal states, including from Florida Republicans Gov. Ron DeSantis and Sen. Rick Scott, who said Florida's coasts must remain off the table.

title: Endangerment Finding Targeted: EPA Moves to Erase Legal Basis for All Climate Rules
synopsis: On July 29, 2025, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin announced a proposed rule to rescind the agency's 2009 endangerment finding — the scientific and legal declaration that greenhouse gases endanger public health and welfare, and the foundation for all U.S. climate regulation under the Clean Air Act. Zeldin called it the largest deregulatory action in the history of America, claiming it would save $52-54 billion annually in compliance costs. If finalized, the repeal would end greenhouse gas limits on vehicle tailpipes, power plants, and industrial sources, and cripple future administrations' ability to regulate CO2 without new congressional legislation. Legal experts noted the 2009 finding had survived numerous court challenges and was grounded in overwhelming scientific consensus.

title: Environmental Justice Program Wiped Out, 168 Staff Placed on Leave
synopsis: On February 6, 2025, the Trump administration placed approximately 168 EPA environmental justice staff on administrative leave and simultaneously pursued reductions at the Justice Department's environmental justice programs. The moves were part of Trump's broad executive orders abolishing diversity, equity, and inclusion programs across the federal government. EPA's FY2026 congressional budget justification, released in June 2025, allocated zero dollars and zero personnel to environmental justice community grants, technical assistance, and Superfund coordination for underserved communities. Environmental groups warned the rollback disproportionately endangered low-income and minority communities living near industrial polluters and Superfund sites.

title: U.S. Lobbies Nations to Kill Global Plastic Pollution Treaty
synopsis: In late July and early August 2025, the Trump administration actively lobbied foreign governments to reject binding caps on plastic production in the final round of UN global plastics treaty negotiations in Geneva. A memo dated July 25, 2025 circulated to countries at the start of talks outlined U.S. red lines explicitly opposing production limits and restrictions on chemical additives, placing Washington in direct opposition to over 100 countries. The U.S. position insisted on a narrow treaty focused solely on waste disposal, not upstream production controls. Without intervention, the OECD projects global plastic production will triple by 2060, choking oceans and accelerating climate change. Small island nations and the EU accused the Trump administration of single-handedly collapsing humanity's best chance at a binding plastics accord.

title: Capitol Breach Begins
synopsis: At approximately 2:12 PM on January 6, 2021, a violent mob of Trump supporters breached the US Capitol building, shattering windows and overwhelming Capitol Police. The rioters sought to halt the certification of the 2020 election results, marking the first time the Capitol was breached since 1814.

title: 140+ Police Officers Injured at Capitol
synopsis: During the January 6, 2021 insurrection, over 140 police officers from the Capitol Police and DC Metropolitan Police Departments sustained injuries. Officers suffered from traumatic brain injuries, cracked ribs, smashed spinal discs, and exposure to chemical irritants deployed by the mob.
